title: Reversing Scattering to Perform Deep-Tissue Optical Imaging and the Current Need for a Suitable Optoelectronic Solution
problem: Biological tissues are highly turbid (mean optical scattering length ~100 microns), preventing high-resolution optical imaging and excitation beyond ~1mm depth; traditional deep-penetrating modalities (X-ray, MRI, ultrasound) lack biochemical sensitivity.
motivation: Deep-tissue optical imaging with biochemical detection capability would revolutionize biomedical research and clinical diagnostics by combining penetration depth of X-ray/MRI/ultrasound with the biochemical specificity of optical methods (fluorescence, harmonic generation, Raman, absorption).
method: Optical scattering-reversal approach that compensates for tissue turbidity by reversing the scattering process, enabling focused light delivery and collection through deep tissue, requiring novel optoelectronic integrated circuits for signal modulation and detection.
key_novelty: Scattering-reversal optical technique to overcome tissue turbidity, enabling deep-tissue high-resolution biochemical imaging.
contributions: Integration of optical and electronic processing
Enabling technology identification for optoelectronic solutions
